references.text: Earlier in the same chapter, the fat to be offered from cattle is described, including the fat that covers the entrails—the same principle applied to small livestock in verse 9.
Repeats the instructions regarding the fat and the fatty tail to be offered from the peace offering, with specific reference to the fat portions covering the entrails.
Describes the removal of fat from the sin offering bull, including the fat that covers the entrails and all the fat on the entrails—parallel terminology.
At the consecration of Aaron and his sons, Moses took the fat, the fatty tail, and all the fat on the entrails—the practical execution of this command.
During Aaron's first priestly service, the fat portions from the bull and the ram, including the fatty tail, were placed upon the breast pieces as a burnt offering.
At the consecration offering, the fatty tail and the fat on the entrails were to be taken from the ram—an early precursor to the instructions in Leviticus.
Complementary details in the instruction specifying which fat portions are to be separated from the peace offering.
Connects the specification of the fat portions with the liturgical action where the fat and the breast are presented together.
Establishes a direct theological parallel by using the procedure for the peace offering as the standard for handling fat in the sin offering.
Confirms that the theological significance of the fat as 'the Lord's portion' remains unchanged between the peace offering and the sin offering.
Clarifies the connection between the sin offering and the peace offering by referring to the lamb as a common reference point.
Uses an identical definition of the placement of the fat to show that 'the Lord's portion' is unchanging across different types of offerings.
Recognizes the theological reason (that the fat belongs to the Lord) behind the practical instructions regarding its removal.
